diz1: A 6-week interactive home exercise programme for knee osteoarthritis: a promise card, a session player that counts aloud, a pain traffic light, a 30-second test and a secret unlocked in every session.
diz4: In knee osteoarthritis, exercise is one of the leading ways to ease pain and improve daily function; the hard part is keeping it up. In this six-week home programme, every session unlocks a secret about your knee or your habits. The questions are visible from the start; the answers open only when you finish the session.

diz124: The reason is usually not a lack of willpower. In a systematic review of treatment adherence in physiotherapy, the factors strongly linked with not keeping up exercise were: increased pain during exercise, low self-confidence, seeing many barriers, little social support, anxiety, depression and a sense of helplessness.
diz125: This programme was built for exactly these: a pain traffic light, small measurable steps, a promise card and someone close you can share your promise with.

diz127: X-rays and pain don’t always tell the same story. A review of studies found that only 15% to 76% of people with knee pain showed osteoarthritis on X-ray, and that 15% to 81% of people with osteoarthritis on X-ray had pain.
diz128: So even if your X-ray looks bad, your knee can get stronger and your pain can ease. The aim of exercise is not the picture on the film; it is your pain and your daily life.
diz129: Source: Bedson and Croft, BMC Musculoskeletal Disorders, 2008
diz130: On the front of your thigh: the quadriceps. Each time your knee bends and straightens as you walk, this muscle takes the load.
diz131: In a meta-analysis of 46,819 people, those with weak quadriceps were about 1.85 times more likely to develop symptomatic knee osteoarthritis if they were women, and 1.43 times if they were men. The quality of the evidence is low; even so, most of the exercises in this programme target this muscle.
diz132: Source: Øiestad et al., British Journal of Sports Medicine, 2022

diz151: The honest answer: noticeable, but not a miracle. In the latest Cochrane review of 139 studies and 12,468 people, exercise compared with no exercise improved pain by about 13 points and daily function by about 12.5 points out of 100 by the end of the programme.

diz157: According to guidelines, morning stiffness in knee osteoarthritis is either absent or lasts less than 30 minutes. Over the age of 45, together with pain that gets worse with activity, the diagnosis can usually be made on examination.
diz158: If your stiffness lasts more than half an hour every morning, or your joints become swollen and warm, tell your doctor; there may be another cause.

diz166: Why was it designed this way?
diz167: Seven science-based tips for keeping up exercise
diz168: A large share of people advised to exercise at home don’t keep the programme up. Every part of this page is based on an idea from research into this problem. We have not used pressure tactics such as guilt, shame or false urgency.
diz170: Plans of the “if this happens, I will do that” kind were linked with a medium-to-large effect on reaching goals.
diz172: Something whose question you know but whose answer you haven’t learnt yet sparks curiosity. Each session ends in a way that makes you curious about the next.
diz174: No penalty for breaking a streak: in habit research, missing a single opportunity did not significantly affect the process.
diz176: Increased pain during exercise is one of the strongest reasons people stop. The light helps you tell acceptable pain apart and adjust the programme.
diz178: The 30-second chair stand test is repeated at the start, in week three and at the end, so you can see your own progress.
diz180: In an experiment, listening to something you enjoy only while exercising clearly increased how often people went to the gym.
diz182: Little social support is one of the factors linked with stopping exercise. You can share your promise with someone close to you.
diz185: Six weeks, two sessions a week. Each session has a one-minute warm-up and four exercises, and each exercise is done in two sets. The number of repetitions in the next session is adjusted to your pain and effort answers at the end of each session.
diz187: Sessions 1–4: Towel press, seated knee straightening, straight leg raise, sit-to-stand from a chair.
diz189: Sessions 5–8: Seated knee straightening, sit-to-stand from a chair, side-lying leg raise, wall half-squat.
diz191: Sessions 9–12: Sit-to-stand with a slow sit, wall half-squat, side-lying leg raise, straight leg raise.

diz200: The programme lasts six weeks with two sessions a week. Leaving at least one day between sessions gives your muscles time to recover. Each session takes about 15 minutes.
diz201: What happens if I miss a session?
diz202: Nothing is lost; the map carries on from where you left off. In habit research, missing a single opportunity did not significantly affect the process. What matters is not missing often.
diz203: What if my pain increases during exercise?
diz204: Pain that stays below 5 out of 10 and settles within a day is acceptable. If the pain goes above 5 or lasts more than 24 hours, mark it on the pain light at the end of the session; the next session will be lighter. If the pain keeps increasing, see your doctor or physiotherapist.

diz208: See your doctor or physiotherapist before starting the programme if:
diz209: You have recently had knee surgery or a knee injury
diz210: You have new swelling, redness and warmth in your knee, or a fever
diz211: You cannot put weight on your knee
diz212: Your pain is getting steadily worse at rest and at night
diz213: You fall often or your balance is very poor
